questions.stem: Which statement best describes the defining functional characteristic of the normal heart?
options: It contracts only during waking hours and rests at night
It pumps blood rhythmically and efficiently, maintaining one-way flow through the circulation
Both ventricles generate identical systolic pressures
It fills entirely by active suction generated by the atria
questions.explanation: The normal heart pumps rhythmically and efficiently, and its valves guarantee one-way blood movement. The two ventricles work at very different pressures, and filling is predominantly passive.
tags: Foundations of Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics

questions.stem: What is the normal pressure range of the right atrium?
questions.explanation: The right atrium is a low-pressure receiving chamber, normally about 0–4 mmHg. Values of 8–12 mmHg are typical of the left atrium, and 25 mmHg approximates pulmonary artery systolic pressure.
tags: Foundations of Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics

questions.stem: What is the approximate normal systolic pressure in the pulmonary artery?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery carries low-pressure blood, with a normal systolic pressure of roughly 25 mmHg. A pressure near 120 mmHg would indicate significant pulmonary hypertension.
tags: Foundations of Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics

questions.stem: What is the normal pressure range of the left atrium?
questions.explanation: The left atrium normally operates at 8–10 mmHg, higher than the right atrium because the pulmonary venous circuit operates at higher pressure than the systemic venous circuit.
tags: Foundations of Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics

questions.stem: What is the approximate normal systolic pressure in the aorta?
questions.explanation: The aorta reflects systemic arterial pressure, normally about 120 mmHg systolic, generated by the left ventricle — the highest-pressure pump of the heart.
tags: Foundations of Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics

questions.stem: Which chamber generates the highest pressure in the heart?
questions.explanation: The left ventricle must eject blood into the high-resistance systemic circulation, generating pressures up to ~120 mmHg. The right ventricle works against the low-resistance pulmonary circuit at about one-fifth of that pressure.
tags: Foundations of Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics

questions.stem: According to pressure–flow relationships, blood in the systemic circulation moves:
options: From low pressure to high pressure
From high pressure to low pressure, down a pressure gradient
At equal pressures throughout the arterial tree
questions.explanation: Hemodynamics are governed by pressure gradients: blood flows from regions of higher pressure to regions of lower pressure. Valves then maintain one-way movement once the blood has been propelled.
tags: Foundations of Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics

questions.stem: What is the primary role of the cardiac valves?
options: To maintain one-way (unidirectional) blood movement through the heart
To generate systolic pressure within the ventricles
To regulate heart rate through mechanoreceptors
To equalize pressures between the atria and ventricles
questions.explanation: Valves exist to keep blood moving in one direction and prevent backward (regurgitant) flow. Pressure is generated by myocardial contraction, not the valves themselves.
tags: Foundations of Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics

questions.stem: The coordinated "ordered sequence" of chamber contraction refers to:
options: Atria contracting before the ventricles, then ventricles ejecting in sequence
Each chamber contracting independently of the others
questions.explanation: Chambers contract in an ordered sequence: atrial systole first tops up ventricular filling, then ventricular systole ejects blood. This sequence is orchestrated by the conduction system.
tags: Foundations of Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics

questions.stem: "Hemodynamics" is best defined as the study of:
options: The electrical conduction properties of the myocardium
The cellular metabolism of heart muscle
The forces (pressure, flow, and resistance) that govern blood movement
The genetic regulation of cardiac development
questions.explanation: Hemodynamics explains pressure–flow relationships: how pressure gradients, vessel resistance, and cardiac pumping interact to move blood. It is the physiological basis for interpreting echo Doppler data.
tags: Foundations of Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics

questions.stem: The right atrium receives venous return directly from:
options: The superior and inferior vena cavae
questions.explanation: Systemic venous return arrives at the right atrium via the SVC and IVC (with a small contribution from the coronary sinus). Pulmonary veins deliver oxygenated blood to the left atrium instead.
tags: Foundations of Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics

questions.stem: The tricuspid valve directs blood from the:
options: Left atrium to the left ventricle
Right atrium to the right ventricle
Right ventricle to the pulmonary artery
questions.explanation: The tricuspid valve is the right-sided AV valve, guiding venous blood from the right atrium into the right ventricle during diastole and closing during systole to prevent regurgitation.
tags: Foundations of Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics

questions.stem: The pulmonary artery is described as carrying:
questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated (venous) blood from the right ventricle to the lungs at low pressure (~25 mmHg systolic), reflecting the low resistance of the pulmonary vascular bed.
tags: Foundations of Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics

questions.stem: The left atrium receives its blood supply from:
questions.explanation: Four pulmonary veins deliver freshly oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. This is the pulmonary "exception" — veins carrying oxygenated blood, and an artery (pulmonary) carrying deoxygenated blood.
tags: Foundations of Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics

questions.stem: Which valve directs left ventricular ejection into the systemic circulation?
questions.explanation: The aortic semilunar valve opens when LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure, directing ejected blood into the aorta. The pulmonary valve performs the equivalent role on the right side.
tags: Foundations of Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics

questions.stem: The pulmonary circulation operates at lower pressure than the systemic circulation primarily because:
options: The right ventricle is stronger than the left ventricle
The pulmonary vascular bed is a short, low-resistance circuit
The lungs store blood under high pressure
questions.explanation: The lungs are adjacent to the heart, so blood travels a short distance through a large, low-resistance capillary bed. Only modest pressures (~25 mmHg) are needed, which is why the RV wall is thin.
tags: Foundations of Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics

questions.stem: A patient presents with jugular venous distension, peripheral edema, and an elevated right atrial pressure of 14 mmHg. These findings are most consistent with:
questions.explanation: Elevated RA pressure with systemic venous congestion (JVD, edema) indicates right-sided decompensation. Left-sided disease produces pulmonary venous congestion (dyspnea, rales) instead.
tags: Foundations of Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics

questions.stem: Why does the right ventricle normally have a much thinner wall than the left ventricle?
options: Pulmonary afterload is much lower than systemic afterload
The right ventricle ejects a smaller stroke volume
The right ventricle contains less muscle protein
The right ventricle never hypertrophies under any condition
questions.explanation: Wall thickness matches workload. Because the pulmonary circuit requires only ~25 mmHg, the RV develops far less pressure than the LV and needs less muscle mass — although it can hypertrophy if pulmonary pressure rises.
tags: Foundations of Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics

questions.stem: Which of the following pressure values corresponds to the pulmonary artery?
questions.explanation: Approximately 25 mmHg is the normal pulmonary artery systolic pressure. The other values correspond to the right atrium (0–4), left atrium (8–10), and aorta (~120).
tags: Foundations of Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares the left and right atrial pressures?
options: The right atrial pressure is higher than the left atrial pressure
Both atria operate at identical pressures
The left atrial pressure (8–10 mmHg) is higher than the right atrial pressure (0–4 mmHg)
questions.explanation: The left side of the heart operates at higher filling pressures (LA 8–10 mmHg) than the right side (RA 0–4 mmHg), consistent with the higher-pressure systemic arterial circuit the left heart feeds. ---
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: The first heart sound (S1) is produced by:
options: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves
Closure of the mitral and tricuspid (AV) valves
questions.explanation: S1 marks the onset of ventricular systole and results from the abrupt closure of the AV valves as ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure.
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: The second heart sound (S2) is produced by:
options: Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle
Turbulent flow across the LV outflow tract
Closure of the semilunar valves at the end of systole
questions.explanation: S2 occurs in isovolumetric relaxation when the aortic and pulmonary valves snap shut as ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure, ending systole.
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: An S3 gallop heard in a 62-year-old patient with dyspnea most likely indicates:
options: Normal aging of the conduction system
Ventricular volume overload or heart failure
questions.explanation: S3 occurs during rapid filling and is normal in children and young adults, but in an older adult it suggests volume overload with poor ventricular compliance — a classic finding in heart failure.
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: The fourth heart sound (S4) is best explained as:
options: The sound of atrial contraction ejecting blood into a stiff, noncompliant ventricle
The opening snap of a stenotic mitral valve
questions.explanation: S4 is generated when the atria contract against a stiff, hypertrophied, or ischemic ventricle late in diastole. It is always pathological in adults and occurs just before S1, shortly after the P wave.
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: According to the lecture, the cardiac cycle officially begins with:
questions.explanation: The cycle begins with the P wave, which depolarizes the atria and initiates atrial systole — the first of the seven phases.
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: Systole is defined as the portion of the cardiac cycle involving:
questions.explanation: Systole encompasses contraction of the ventricles and ejection of the stroke volume. Diastole encompasses relaxation and filling.
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: Diastole is defined as the portion of the cardiac cycle involving:
options: The QRS complex and the plateau phase
Relaxation and filling of the ventricles
questions.explanation: During diastole the ventricles relax (isovolumetric relaxation) and then fill passively and actively, ending with atrial systole before the next contraction.
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: How many phases are conventionally used to describe the pressure changes of the cardiac cycle?
questions.explanation: Seven phases describe the cycle: atrial systole, isovolumetric contraction, rapid ejection, reduced ejection, isovolumetric relaxation, rapid filling, and reduced filling.
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: Within the seven-phase model, transitions from one phase to the next are defined by:
options: The duration of the QT interval
questions.explanation: Valve events define phase boundaries: AV closure starts isovolumetric contraction, semilunar opening starts ejection, semilunar closure starts isovolumetric relaxation, and AV opening starts rapid filling.
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: At a resting heart rate of 75 bpm, systole occupies approximately what proportion of the cardiac cycle?
questions.explanation: At 75 bpm the cycle lasts 0.8 seconds: roughly 0.3 seconds of systole (about one-third) and 0.5 seconds of diastole (about two-thirds).
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: When heart rate increases significantly, which portion of the cardiac cycle is shortened the most?
questions.explanation: Increasing heart rate compresses diastole far more than systole, reducing filling time and coronary perfusion time — a key reason extreme tachycardia reduces stroke volume.
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: Which statement about the electrical–mechanical relationship is correct?
options: Ventricular contraction occurs before the QRS complex
The ECG records the mechanical contraction of the heart
Electrical activation (the QRS) precedes mechanical contraction by a brief interval
The P wave marks the onset of ventricular ejection
questions.explanation: The ECG records electrical events, which trigger — but are not themselves — mechanical events. Ventricular contraction begins just after the QRS complex during isovolumetric contraction.
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: Which phase of the cardiac cycle begins immediately after the QRS complex?
questions.explanation: Ventricular depolarization (QRS) triggers contraction; because all valves are briefly closed, pressure rises without volume change — isovolumetric contraction.
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: Atrial systole begins shortly after which ECG event?
questions.explanation: The P wave depolarizes the atria, and atrial contraction follows immediately, producing the final "atrial kick" of ventricular filling.
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: At the onset of ventricular filling (phase 6), left ventricular pressure is closest to:
questions.explanation: The relaxed ventricle has just finished isovolumetric relaxation, so its pressure is near 0 mmHg, well below atrial pressure — which is precisely why the AV valves open and passive filling begins.
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: The first heart sound is best auscultated at which location?
options: The cardiac apex (fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line)
The back, below the left scapula
questions.explanation: S1 (AV valve closure) is loudest at the apex, where the mitral valve closure is best transmitted. S2 is best heard at the base (upper right sternal border).
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: The second heart sound is best heard at:
options: The base of the heart (upper sternal borders)
questions.explanation: S2 (semilunar valve closure) is transmitted best to the base of the heart, especially the right upper sternal border (aortic component).
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: Physiological splitting of S2 occurs during:
questions.explanation: Inspiration increases venous return and delays pulmonary valve closure, creating a wider A2–P2 split. This is a normal finding that disappears with expiration.
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: A systolic murmur would be timed between:
questions.explanation: Systole runs from S1 (AV closure) to S2 (semilunar closure), so a murmur between S1 and S2 is systolic — e.g., aortic stenosis or mitral regurgitation.
tags: Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle Overview

questions.stem: A murmur heard between S2 and the following S1, such as that of mitral stenosis, is classified as:
questions.explanation: The interval from S2 to the next S1 is diastole; murmurs occurring there — like the diastolic rumble of mitral stenosis or the early diastolic decrescendo of aortic regurgitation — are diastolic murmurs. ---
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: In a healthy resting adult, the "atrial kick" contributes approximately what fraction of ventricular filling?
questions.explanation: Most ventricular filling is passive; the atrial contraction adds the final 20–30% of the EDV. This fraction becomes critically important when the ventricle is stiff or when filling is obstructed.
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: The "a wave" seen in an atrial pressure tracing corresponds to:
questions.explanation: Atrial systole forces pressure up inside the atrium, producing the a wave. Cannon a waves in the JVP reflect atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve (e.g., complete heart block).
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: A patient with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy develops atrial fibrillation and suddenly deteriorates. The most likely reason is:
options: Loss of the atrial kick, which was providing a large share of filling to a stiff ventricle
Sudden closure of the semilunar valves
Excessive passive filling through a widened mitral orifice
questions.explanation: In stiff ventricles (HCM, restrictive disease, mitral stenosis) the atrial kick supplies an outsized fraction of filling. Atrial fibrillation eliminates this kick, dropping EDV, stroke volume, and cardiac output.
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: During phase 1 (atrial systole), the AV valves are:
options: Alternating open and closed with each beat
questions.explanation: Atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure during atrial systole, so the mitral and tricuspid valves remain open, allowing the atria to eject their contents into the relaxed ventricles.
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: End-diastolic volume (EDV) is reached at the end of:
questions.explanation: The atrial contraction tops off the ventricle, completing end-diastolic volume just before the QRS. This maximal ventricular volume defines preload.
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: "Preload" is most directly related to:
questions.explanation: Preload is the end-diastolic wall stress or stretch of the ventricle, operationally equated with EDV or end-diastolic pressure. It sets the sarcomere length before contraction begins.
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: During phase 2 (isovolumetric contraction), the status of the four valves is:
options: AV valves open, semilunar valves closed
AV valves closed, semilunar valves open
questions.explanation: Immediately after the QRS, ventricular pressure has exceeded atrial pressure (closing the AV valves) but has not yet reached arterial pressure (semilunar valves still closed) — all four valves are shut.
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: The term "isovolumetric" during phase 2 refers to the fact that:
options: Blood volume in the body is constant
Ventricular volume does not change while pressure rises
questions.explanation: With all valves closed, no blood can enter or leave the ventricles; the ventricle contracts against a fixed volume, so pressure rises steeply with no change in ventricular volume.
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: The mitral component of the first heart sound (M1) represents:
options: Closure of the mitral valve at the start of isovolumetric contraction
Closure of the tricuspid valve only
questions.explanation: As LV pressure rises above LA pressure, the mitral valve closes, producing M1 — the louder first component of S1, heard best at the apex.
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: Immediately after the QRS complex, left ventricular pressure:
options: Rises rapidly while volume remains constant
questions.explanation: Phase 2 is isovolumetric contraction: the LV contracts against closed valves, so pressure climbs steeply (from ~8 to ~80 mmHg in the LV) while volume stays fixed at EDV.
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: The "c wave" in the venous/atrial pressure waveform results from:
options: Bulging of the AV valve back into the atrium as the ventricle contracts
questions.explanation: At the onset of ventricular systole, the closed AV valve bulges back toward the atrium, briefly raising atrial pressure — the c wave.
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: The first heart sound coincides with the beginning of:
questions.explanation: AV valve closure (S1) is the event that initiates phase 2, isovolumetric contraction, so S1 and this phase begin together.
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: The dicrotic notch seen on an arterial pressure tracing is caused by:
questions.explanation: When the aortic valve closes, a brief rebound of pressure against the closed valve produces the dicrotic notch on the descending limb of the arterial waveform — marking the end of systole.
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: Phase 3 (rapid ejection) begins when:
options: Ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure
Ventricular pressure exceeds the pressure in the great arteries
questions.explanation: Rapid ejection starts the instant LV (or RV) pressure surpasses aortic (or pulmonary) pressure, forcing the semilunar valves open.
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: Opening of the aortic and pulmonary valves defines the transition into:
questions.explanation: Semilunar valve opening marks the end of isovolumetric contraction and the beginning of the rapid ejection phase, during which most of the stroke volume leaves the ventricle.
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: During ejection, the stroke volume ejected represents approximately:
questions.explanation: A normal ventricle ejects roughly two-thirds of its EDV (e.g., ejecting 70 mL from an EDV of ~110–120 mL), leaving an ESV of about 40–50 mL.
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: Ejection fraction is calculated as:
questions.explanation: EF is the percentage of EDV ejected per beat: (EDV − ESV) ÷ EDV × 100. It is the most widely used echo index of systolic function.
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: The normal range for left ventricular ejection fraction is:
questions.explanation: A normal LVEF is roughly 55–70%. Values below 40% define significantly reduced systolic function; values above 70% may indicate a hyperdynamic state.
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: A patient's EDV is 120 mL and ESV is 50 mL. What is the stroke volume?
questions.explanation: SV = EDV − ESV = 120 − 50 = 70 mL (with an EF of 70 ÷ 120 ≈ 58%).
tags: Phases 1–2: Atrial Systole and Isovolumetric Contraction

questions.stem: During phases 3 and 4 (ejection), the AV valves remain:
options: Closed, preventing regurgitation into the atria
questions.explanation: Throughout systole, ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure, keeping the mitral and tricuspid valves closed so ejected blood can only exit through the semilunar valves. ---

questions.stem: During rapid ejection, aortic pressure:
options: Rises quickly toward ~120 mmHg as blood is expelled into the aorta
questions.explanation: Stroke volume ejected into the aorta raises arterial pressure rapidly to its systolic peak (~120 mmHg). This is the systemic "pressure rise" seen on arterial tracings during phase 3.

questions.stem: During phase 4 (reduced ejection), ejection slows because:
options: The semilunar valves have already closed
The pressure gradient between ventricle and artery is narrowing as the ventricle begins to relax
Atrial pressure has exceeded ventricular pressure
questions.explanation: As ventricular contraction wanes and the ventricle starts to repolarize, ventricular pressure falls toward arterial pressure, shrinking the ejection gradient and slowing outflow — though the semilunar valves are still open.

questions.stem: The T wave of the ECG typically occurs during which phase?
questions.explanation: Ventricular repolarization (T wave) occurs while ejection is winding down, in reduced ejection — shortly before the semilunar valves close.

questions.stem: While the ventricles are ejecting, atrial pressure gradually rises because:
options: Venous return continues to fill the closed atria (producing the v wave)
questions.explanation: With the AV valves shut during systole, venous return accumulates in the atria, raising atrial pressure — the v wave on the pressure tracing.

questions.stem: The volume of blood remaining in the ventricle at the end of systole is called the:
questions.explanation: ESV is the ventricular volume remaining after ejection. EDV − ESV = stroke volume, and the ESV–afterload relationship is central to interpreting the PV loop.

questions.stem: An ejection fraction of 25% indicates:
options: Isolated diastolic dysfunction with preserved ejection
questions.explanation: An EF of 25% is far below the normal 55–70% range and indicates severe impairment of systolic pump function, consistent with dilated cardiomyopathy or advanced heart failure.

questions.stem: Phase 5 (isovolumetric relaxation) begins:
options: When the ventricle begins contracting after the QRS
After ventricular repolarization, when the semilunar valves close abruptly
questions.explanation: As the ventricle repolarizes and relaxes, its pressure falls below arterial pressure and the semilunar valves close (S2) — with the AV valves still closed, beginning isovolumetric relaxation.

questions.stem: The second heart sound (S2) is generated at the start of:
questions.explanation: Semilunar valve closure produces S2 and defines the boundary between reduced ejection and isovolumetric relaxation.

questions.stem: The defining feature of phase 5 is that:
options: Ventricular volume increases while pressure rises
Ventricular pressure falls without any change in ventricular volume
questions.explanation: With all valves closed, the relaxing ventricle loses pressure rapidly but cannot change volume — the mirror image of isovolumetric contraction.

questions.stem: On an arterial pressure waveform, the dicrotic notch appears:
options: At the start of rapid ejection
On the descending limb at the time of aortic valve closure
questions.explanation: The notch reflects a brief pressure rebound when the aortic valve closes at the end of systole, corresponding to S2.

questions.stem: Phase 6 (rapid filling) begins when:
options: Ventricular pressure drops below atrial pressure
questions.explanation: The moment LV pressure falls below the atrial pressure accumulated during systole, the AV valves open and passive filling begins.

questions.stem: Which valve event marks the beginning of rapid ventricular filling?
options: Opening of the mitral and tricuspid valves
questions.explanation: AV valve opening ends isovolumetric relaxation and starts phase 6, the period of fastest passive ventricular filling.

questions.stem: The majority of normal ventricular filling occurs:
questions.explanation: Approximately 70–80% of filling happens passively early in diastole as the relaxed ventricle "sucks" blood from the atria; the atrial kick contributes the remaining 20–30%.

questions.stem: The third heart sound (S3) occurs during:
questions.explanation: S3 is the soft sound of rapid early-diastolic filling vibrating the ventricular walls. Normal in the young, it signals volume overload or failure in adults.

questions.stem: Phase 7 (reduced filling, or diastasis) is characterized by:
options: A steep rise in ventricular pressure
A slowing of filling as the pressure gradient between atrium and ventricle becomes smaller
questions.explanation: As the ventricle fills, its pressure approaches atrial pressure, so the gradient — and therefore the filling rate — diminishes until the next P wave.

questions.stem: Late in diastole, the ventricles become:
options: Less compliant, so additional filling raises pressure more steeply
questions.explanation: Ventricular compliance falls as the chamber approaches its volume limit; late-diastolic filling occurs on the steeper portion of the pressure–volume curve, so pressure rises faster.

questions.stem: The cardiac cycle is restarted at the end of phase 7 by:
options: The next P wave initiating atrial systole
questions.explanation: Reduced filling continues until the SA node fires again: the next P wave depolarizes the atria, restarting the cycle with phase 1.

questions.stem: During significant tachycardia, which phase of the cardiac cycle is progressively eliminated first?
questions.explanation: Diastasis is sacrificed first as heart rate rises; with further shortening, rapid filling time is also encroached upon, eventually reducing EDV and stroke volume.

questions.stem: A patient with fever-induced tachycardia at 140 bpm would primarily lose:
options: The diastolic filling time, especially diastasis
questions.explanation: Tachycardia compresses diastole; the filling phases (6 and 7) shorten most, reducing EDV, preload, and ultimately stroke volume and cardiac output.

questions.stem: A normal left ventricular end-diastolic pressure is approximately:
questions.explanation: LVEDP normally sits around 8–12 mmHg, slightly above RA pressure. Elevated LVEDP indicates increased filling pressure — from volume overload or diastolic stiffness. ---
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: The pressure–volume loop is most commonly applied to which ventricle?
questions.explanation: Although the concept applies to any chamber, the PV loop is conventionally used for the LV because its high-pressure cycle is best characterized and clinically relevant.
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: A pressure–volume loop plots a single point-set representing:
questions.explanation: Each closed loop represents one cardiac cycle: filling, isovolumetric contraction, ejection, and isovolumetric relaxation, with pressure on the y-axis and volume on the x-axis.
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: The width of the pressure–volume loop represents:
questions.explanation: The horizontal width of the loop is the difference between EDV and ESV — the stroke volume ejected during that beat.
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: A normal pressure–volume loop is traversed in which direction?
options: It does not have a direction
questions.explanation: The LV loop moves counterclockwise: rightward along the bottom (filling), upward on the left side (isovolumetric contraction), leftward along the top (ejection), and downward on the right side (isovolumetric relaxation).
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: Segment A of the PV loop corresponds to:
options: Ventricular filling along the end-diastolic pressure–volume relationship
questions.explanation: Segment A traces the filling phase from mitral valve opening to EDV, following the end-diastolic pressure–volume curve.
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: Segment B (the vertical, right-sided rise) corresponds to:
questions.explanation: The steep upward segment at constant volume (EDV) is isovolumetric contraction: pressure soars from ~8 to ~80 mmHg with no change in volume.
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: Segment C (the top, leftward-moving segment) corresponds to:
questions.explanation: During ejection, volume falls as pressure continues to rise briefly then falls — the loop's top segment, running from EDV to ESV with the semilunar valves open.
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: Segment D (the vertical, left-sided descent) corresponds to:
questions.explanation: After semilunar valve closure at ESV, pressure falls steeply with no volume change — isovolumetric relaxation — until the AV valves open at the loop's bottom-left corner.
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: EDV and ESV define which parameter on the pressure–volume loop?
options: The horizontal extremes that determine stroke volume
questions.explanation: The loop's right border is EDV and its left border is ESV; their difference is stroke volume, the loop's width.
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: The slope of the end-diastolic pressure–volume relationship (EDPVR) is inversely related to:
questions.explanation: The EDPVR slope rises as the ventricle stiffens: a steep EDPVR means low compliance (small volume change causes large pressure rise), as in hypertrophic or restrictive disease.
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: The slope of the end-systolic pressure–volume relationship (ESPVR) is an index of:
questions.explanation: The ESPVR slope (Ees) is the classic load-independent measure of contractility: steeper slope = stronger ventricle, shallower slope = depressed inotropy.
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: Increasing preload alone (e.g., by fluid infusion) produces which change in the PV loop?
options: A wider loop shifted rightward, with increased stroke volume and an unchanged ESPVR
A taller loop with decreased stroke volume
A narrower loop with decreased stroke volume
questions.explanation: More filling increases EDV, and via Frank–Starling the ventricle ejects more — widening the loop. The ESPVR (contractility) slope itself does not change.
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: Increasing afterload alone produces which change in the PV loop?
options: Increased stroke volume with a wider loop
A taller loop reaching higher pressure with a reduced stroke volume
questions.explanation: With greater resistance, the ventricle ejects less (higher ESV) and reaches higher systolic pressure: the loop grows taller and narrower, with reduced stroke volume.
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: Increasing contractility (inotropy) produces which change in the PV loop?
options: A shallower ESPVR with lower stroke volume
A steeper ESPVR and increased stroke volume (larger loop width)
A rightward shift of the EDPVR
questions.explanation: Enhanced contractility steepens the end-systolic relationship: the ventricle ejects to a smaller ESV, widening the loop and increasing stroke volume.
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: The point on the PV loop where the semilunar valves close corresponds to:
options: End-systolic volume, the start of isovolumetric relaxation
questions.explanation: Semilunar closure occurs at ESV, the top-left corner of the loop, initiating the vertical isovolumetric relaxation segment.
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: The upper-left corner of the pressure–volume loop (end of ejection) represents:
questions.explanation: The end-systolic point (ESV + end-systolic pressure) lies on the ESPVR and is the reference point for contractility analysis.
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: A patient with severe LV hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction would demonstrate:
options: An EDPVR shifted up and to the left (steeper), with elevated filling pressures at low volumes
An ESPVR parallel to the volume axis
questions.explanation: A stiff, hypertrophied ventricle generates high diastolic pressures even at small volumes: the EDPVR steepens/shifts up-left, the hallmark of diastolic dysfunction.
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: In a dilated cardiomyopathy, the EDPVR is characteristically:
options: Shifted to the right, reflecting larger ventricular volumes
questions.explanation: Remodeling and dilation increase the operating chamber volumes, shifting the EDPVR rightward — the loop widens even as contractility (ESPVR slope) falls.
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: The area enclosed within the pressure–volume loop approximates:
options: The external (stroke) work performed by the ventricle per beat
questions.explanation: The loop area equals pressure × volume work — the external stroke work per beat. The total energy cost also includes internal work (isovolumetric tension) needed for oxygen demand calculations.
tags: Phases 5–7 — Isovolumetric Relaxation, Rapid and Reduced Filling

questions.stem: If preload increases while afterload and contractility remain constant, stroke volume will:
options: Stay exactly the same in all circumstances
Increase according to the Frank–Starling relationship
questions.explanation: Greater end-diastolic stretch produces a stronger contraction and larger stroke volume (Frank–Starling), up to the point of excessive stretch. ---

questions.stem: Preload is best defined as:
options: The arterial resistance the ventricle ejects against
The strength of myocardial contraction independent of stretch
The degree of ventricular wall stress or stretch at end-diastole, just before contraction
The pressure generated during isovolumetric relaxation
questions.explanation: Preload is the end-diastolic "load" on the ventricle — the stretch of myocytes set by EDV/EDP. It determines initial sarcomere length and thereby contraction strength.

questions.stem: Clinically, LV preload is most often estimated by:
options: End-diastolic volume or LV end-diastolic pressure (often approximated by PCWP)
questions.explanation: Preload is operationally assessed with EDV, LVEDP, or surrogate filling pressures such as the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (reflecting LA pressure).

questions.stem: The Frank–Starling law states that:
options: Stroke volume falls as end-diastolic volume rises
Within physiologic limits, stroke volume increases as end-diastolic fiber stretch (preload) increases
Stroke volume is independent of preload
Contractility depends only on heart rate
questions.explanation: Increased preload stretches myocytes toward the optimal actin–myosin overlap, generating greater force and a larger stroke volume — the intrinsic autoregulation of output.

questions.stem: The sarcomere length that produces maximal tension in cardiac muscle is approximately:
questions.explanation: Maximal cross-bridge formation occurs near 2.0–2.2 µm sarcomere length. Stretching beyond this reduces overlap and falls onto the descending limb of the length–tension curve.

questions.stem: Acute hemorrhage with hypotension will produce which change in LV preload?
options: Decreased preload due to reduced circulating volume and venous return
No change until blood pressure falls below 60 mmHg
questions.explanation: Volume loss reduces venous return and EDV, lowering preload and stroke volume via the Frank–Starling mechanism until compensation (venoconstriction, tachycardia) intervenes.

questions.stem: The pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) is used clinically to estimate:
options: Left atrial pressure and LV filling (preload) pressure
questions.explanation: Wedging a catheter in a distal pulmonary artery allows the LA pressure to be transmitted backward, so PCWP approximates LA/LV end-diastolic filling pressure.

questions.stem: On echocardiography, right atrial pressure (a preload surrogate) is estimated using:
options: IVC diameter and its collapsibility with respiration/sniff
questions.explanation: A dilated IVC (>2.1 cm) with <50% inspiratory collapse suggests elevated RA pressure; a small, fully collapsing IVC suggests low RA pressure (low preload).

questions.stem: Rapid intravenous fluid bolus administration will:
options: Increase preload and, via Frank–Starling, increase stroke volume
Have no effect on the ventricles
questions.explanation: Expanding blood volume increases venous return, EDV, and preload, raising stroke volume through the Frank–Starling mechanism (unless the ventricle is on the flat/overstretched part of its curve).

questions.stem: A patient with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has an LVEDP of 24 mmHg despite a normal EDV. The explanation is:
options: Reduced ventricular compliance — a stiff ventricle generates high pressure at a given volume
questions.explanation: In a noncompliant ventricle, the EDPVR is steep: a normal filling volume produces abnormally high end-diastolic pressure. This is diastolic dysfunction, not hypervolemia.

questions.stem: Sustained tachycardia reduces preload primarily by:
questions.explanation: With less time for passive and active filling, EDV falls; preload, stroke volume, and cardiac output are all reduced — the mechanism behind the effect of rate-control in rapid AF.

questions.stem: Loss of the atrial kick (e.g., atrial fibrillation) typically reduces ventricular filling by:
options: Eliminating the 20–30% contribution of atrial contraction to EDV
Increasing passive filling to compensate fully
questions.explanation: Without coordinated atrial contraction, the ventricle loses the "topping-up" portion of its EDV — especially consequential when the ventricle is stiff or outflow is obstructed.

questions.stem: Mitral stenosis causes which preload change in the left ventricle?
options: Increased LV preload due to backflow
Decreased LV preload due to impaired LA-to-LV transfer of blood
questions.explanation: The stenotic mitral orifice obstructs filling, so the LV underfills (decreased preload), while LA pressure rises — explaining pulmonary congestion with a small, underfilled LV.

questions.stem: "Inflow resistance" as a preload factor refers to:
options: Resistance to blood entering the ventricle (e.g., across the AV valves or through venous pathways)
Resistance to ejection into the aorta
questions.explanation: Obstruction along the venous return pathway (e.g., mitral stenosis, tricuspid stenosis, SVC obstruction) reduces ventricular filling and therefore preload.

questions.stem: Increased outflow resistance (e.g., severe aortic stenosis) affects preload how?
options: It has no relationship to preload
It reduces preload by accelerating emptying
It raises LV end-diastolic pressure (preload pressure) as blood backs up because ejection is impeded
questions.explanation: When the ventricle cannot empty fully against elevated outflow resistance, residual volume accumulates and filling pressures rise over time — chronically elevating preload pressures.

questions.stem: In experimental settings, the most direct measures of preload are:
options: LV end-diastolic volume and left atrial pressure
questions.explanation: Direct preload measures are end-diastolic volume and filling pressure; echo surrogates are LV dimensions/volumes and transmitral filling patterns.

questions.stem: Which intervention will decrease preload?
questions.explanation: Venodilation increases venous capacitance, pooling blood peripherally, reducing venous return and ventricular preload — the basis of nitrate therapy in pulmonary congestion.

questions.stem: The skeletal muscle pump during exercise raises preload by:
options: Compressing veins rhythmically to propel venous blood back toward the heart
questions.explanation: Rhythmic muscle contraction plus one-way venous valves pumps blood centrally, increasing venous return and EDV during dynamic exercise.

questions.stem: A hypovolemic trauma patient is given a fluid challenge. The expected hemodynamic response is:
options: Rising heart rate with falling stroke volume
Rising PCWP and rising cardiac output as preload is restored
questions.explanation: Fluid restores intravascular volume, raising venous return, EDV/PCWP, and stroke volume — reflected as increased cardiac output.

questions.stem: The filling (preload) period of each beat ends when:
options: The mitral (AV) valves close at the onset of isovolumetric contraction
questions.explanation: Once the QRS triggers contraction and the AV valves close, no further filling can occur: EDV is fixed and the preload "period" is over.

questions.stem: Which of the following increases LV preload the most?
options: Hypervolemia from renal failure with fluid retention
questions.explanation: Volume retention expands venous return and EDV maximally. Diuretics, dehydration, and hemorrhage all lower preload instead. ---

questions.stem: The single most important determinant of ventricular preload is:
options: Venous return, driven by circulating blood volume
questions.explanation: Preload is essentially the filling the ventricle receives; venous return (determined by blood volume, venous tone, and pumps that return blood to the heart) is the dominant factor.

questions.stem: Severe tricuspid regurgitation contributes to right ventricular preload by:
options: Allowing systolic backflow into the right atrium, which is then re-ejected in the next beat, increasing effective RV volume load
Having no effect on the right ventricle
questions.explanation: In TR, blood regurgitates into the RA during systole, and the enlarged RA volume is delivered back to the RV in diastole — increasing RV end-diastolic volume (right-sided preload/volume overload).

questions.stem: Which of the following decreases ventricular compliance and therefore raises filling pressure at a given volume?
questions.explanation: Fibrosis, hypertrophy, and infiltrative disease stiffen the ventricular wall. The result is a steep EDPVR: high pressures with normal or even reduced volumes.

questions.stem: On echocardiography, the ratio most commonly used to estimate LV filling pressure is:
options: The E/e′ ratio (mitral inflow E velocity to tissue Doppler annular e′ velocity)
questions.explanation: E/e′ correlates with LA pressure/LVEDP: elevated ratios (e.g., >14–15 average) indicate elevated filling pressures — an echo estimate of preload pressure.

questions.stem: Diuretic therapy reduces preload by:
options: Decreasing circulating blood volume and venous return
questions.explanation: By promoting sodium and water excretion, diuretics shrink intravascular volume, reduce venous return and EDV, and lower filling pressures in congested patients.

questions.stem: Cardiac tamponade reduces preload because:
options: Pericardial fluid under pressure compresses all chambers and equalizes diastolic pressures, restricting ventricular filling
questions.explanation: Fluid in the pericardial space limits chamber expansion; venous return is impeded, EDV falls, and preload collapses — producing the classic low-output state with equalized chamber pressures.

questions.stem: Positive-pressure mechanical ventilation tends to:
options: Reduce venous return to the heart by raising intrathoracic pressure
Increase preload only in the right ventricle
questions.explanation: Positive intrathoracic pressure compresses the vena cavae and reduces the pressure gradient driving venous return, lowering preload — one reason hypovolemic patients become hypotensive on ventilators.

questions.stem: Sudden standing from a supine position produces which immediate preload change?
options: A transient decrease in preload due to venous pooling in the legs
No change, because blood volume is constant
Preload rises because the heart is lower
questions.explanation: Gravity pools blood in the lower extremities when upright, temporarily cutting venous return and preload until baroreflex-mediated venoconstriction and tachycardia compensate.

questions.stem: A dilated IVC (>2.1 cm) with minimal respiratory collapse suggests:
options: A normal preload in every patient
questions.explanation: A plethoric, non-collapsing IVC indicates elevated RA pressure. Context matters (e.g., in tamponade or RV failure), but the echo finding itself signals high right-sided filling pressure.

questions.stem: In atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response, LV preload is reduced because of:
options: Both loss of the atrial kick and severely shortened diastolic filling time
Mitral valve stenosis that develops acutely
questions.explanation: Rapid AF removes the atrial contribution to filling and slashes the time available for passive filling, collapsing EDV and stroke volume — the mechanism of decompensation in rapid AF.

questions.stem: The atrial kick is most important hemodynamically in patients with:
options: Stiff, noncompliant ventricles or inflow obstruction (e.g., HCM, mitral stenosis)
questions.explanation: When the ventricle is stiff or filling is obstructed, passive filling contributes less and the atrial contraction supplies a much larger share of EDV; losing it (as in AF) is poorly tolerated.

questions.stem: Symptoms of mitral stenosis classically worsen with tachycardia because:
options: The shortened diastole allows less time for blood to cross the stenotic valve
questions.explanation: Filling across a stenotic mitral valve requires time; tachycardia shortens diastole, raising LA pressure and causing pulmonary congestion. Rate control is a cornerstone of MS management.

questions.stem: "Preload responsiveness" in a hypotensive patient refers to:
options: The patient's heart rate response to atropine
The ability of the ventricle to relax quickly
Whether additional fluid volume will produce a meaningful increase in stroke volume
questions.explanation: A preload-responsive patient sits on the steep portion of the Frank–Starling curve: extra volume raises EDV and stroke volume substantially. A fluid-refractory patient sits on the flat portion.

questions.stem: A patient with severe LV systolic failure has an EDV of 250 mL but a stroke volume of only 30 mL. This illustrates:
options: A failing ventricle on the flat portion of the Starling curve — high preload but little recruitable stroke volume
questions.explanation: In advanced heart failure the dilated ventricle operates at the flat/upper portion of the curve; further preload does not increase output, and high filling pressures produce congestion instead.

questions.stem: Right ventricular preload is normally best represented numerically by:
questions.explanation: RA pressure (0–4 mmHg) is the filling pressure of the RV and is measured or estimated (central venous pressure, echo IVC assessment) to gauge right-sided preload.

questions.stem: Pulmonary venous congestion with dyspnea and rales reflects elevation of:
options: Left atrial (LV filling) pressure causing fluid transudation into the lung interstitium
questions.explanation: When LA pressure rises (increased LV preload pressure or stiffness), the pressure backs into the pulmonary venous bed and capillary pressure exceeds oncotic thresholds, producing edema and dyspnea.

questions.stem: Which drug class acts predominantly by reducing preload through venodilation?
questions.explanation: Nitrates primarily dilate the venous capacitance vessels, pooling blood peripherally, lowering venous return and preload; arterial vasodilators (hydralazine, ACE inhibitors) mainly reduce afterload.

questions.stem: During a Valsalva strain (forced expiration against a closed glottis), venous return and preload:
options: Decrease because raised intrathoracic pressure impedes venous return
Are unaffected because blood volume cannot change
questions.explanation: The increased intrathoracic pressure squeezes down venous return; preload and stroke volume fall, followed by a baroreflex-mediated tachycardia — the basis of the Valsalva response test.

questions.stem: A passive leg raise is performed to test preload responsiveness because it:
options: Autotransfuses pooled leg venous blood centrally, transiently increasing preload
questions.explanation: Raising the legs returns a few hundred milliliters of venous blood to the central circulation — a reversible "fluid challenge" whose stroke volume response reveals preload reserve.

questions.stem: The patient with right ventricular infarction is typically preload-dependent because:
options: The infarcted, poorly contracting RV needs high filling pressures to maintain output, and excessive fluids or nitrates can be harmful
questions.explanation: A stunned RV generates lower pressures and depends on adequate venous return; both underfilling (nitrates/diuretics) and overfilling (dilating the RV beyond pericardial limits) worsen output. ---
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: Afterload is best defined as:
options: The volume of blood in the ventricle at end-diastole
The strength of contraction independent of load
The pressure in the atria during filling
The ventricular wall stress the muscle must generate during ejection — the resistance the ventricle pumps against
questions.explanation: Afterload is the systolic load: arterial impedance, vascular resistance, valve obstruction, and wall stress. Increased afterload makes ejection harder and reduces SV for a given contractility.
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: For the left ventricle, afterload is clinically approximated by:
options: Systemic vascular resistance and arterial (mean/blood) pressure
questions.explanation: Systemic vascular resistance (SVR) and arterial pressure represent the impedance the LV faces; for the RV, pulmonary vascular resistance and PA pressure serve the same role.
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: According to the Laplace relationship, ventricular wall stress is proportional to:
questions.explanation: Wall stress rises with chamber pressure and radius, and falls with wall thickness. Dilation (larger radius) or hypertension (higher pressure) increases stress; hypertrophy (thicker wall) reduces it.
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: In a dilated cardiomyopathy, wall stress increases primarily because:
options: The increased chamber radius raises stress even at the same pressure
questions.explanation: By Laplace's law, a larger radius (dilated ventricle) demands greater wall stress for the same pressure — increasing oxygen demand and worsening the dilated heart's efficiency.
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: Ventricular hypertrophy is a chronic adaptation to increased afterload because:
options: Adding sarcomeres in parallel thickens the wall, reducing wall stress per unit muscle
questions.explanation: Thickening the wall distributes the same pressure over more muscle, lowering wall stress per fiber. The trade-off is reduced compliance and higher oxygen demand.
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: An acute increase in afterload (e.g., sudden severe hypertension) produces:
options: An increased ESV and decreased stroke volume for that beat
No change until the ventricle hypertrophies
questions.explanation: Immediately, the ventricle cannot empty as completely against higher resistance: ESV rises and SV falls (afterload mismatch), unless compensated by greater contractility or preload.
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: Chronic systemic hypertension leads to which ventricular adaptation?
questions.explanation: The chronically pressure-loaded LV adds sarcomeres in parallel, producing concentric LVH — visible on echo as increased wall thickness with normal or reduced cavity size.
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: Chronic pulmonary hypertension produces which ventricular adaptation?
options: Right ventricular hypertrophy (and eventual dilation and failure)
questions.explanation: The RV, forced to eject against elevated pulmonary resistance, hypertrophies; with time it dilates and fails — the echo picture of pulmonary heart disease (cor pulmonale).
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: Severe aortic stenosis increases LV afterload because:
options: The stenotic valve creates a fixed obstruction, so the LV must generate very high intracavitary pressure to eject
questions.explanation: The narrowed orifice is a fixed resistance: the LV must build supraphysiologic pressures (often >200 mmHg) to force blood through, markedly raising wall stress and oxygen demand.
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: Which class of drugs reduces afterload and thereby improves stroke volume in heart failure?
questions.explanation: Arterial vasodilation lowers the resistance the LV ejects against, increasing SV and forward CO while reducing wall stress — the basis of afterload-reducing therapy in systolic heart failure.
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: In a patient with normal blood pressure but severe aortic stenosis, LV afterload is:
options: Low, because the blood pressure is normal
Elevated, because the fixed valve obstruction — not arterial pressure alone — determines the ejection load
questions.explanation: Afterload includes total impedance to ejection, not just arterial pressure. The stenotic valve adds a large fixed component; measuring arterial pressure alone underestimates the true load.
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: In septic shock, SVR collapses. The resulting cardiac findings are:
options: Low afterload with high stroke volume and a hyperdynamic LV on echo
High afterload with low stroke volume
questions.explanation: Vasodilatory shock drops systemic resistance; the LV faces minimal afterload and typically ejects a large stroke volume (hyperdynamic, EF often normal or high) despite the patient's hypotension.
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: Aortic regurgitation produces which combined hemodynamic burden on the LV?
options: Volume (preload) overload — regurgitant flow returns in diastole, raising EDV — plus a large total ejection volume
Pure pressure (afterload) overload with a small cavity
questions.explanation: In AR the LV receives the entire cardiac output of the lungs plus regurgitant aortic flow, markedly increasing EDV and total stroke volume — a chronic volume-overload state leading to eccentric hypertrophy.
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: The relationship between afterload and myocardial oxygen demand is:
options: Afterload does not affect oxygen consumption
Higher afterload (higher wall tension) increases myocardial oxygen demand
Oxygen demand depends only on heart rate
questions.explanation: Wall tension is a principal determinant of MVO2; pressures and radii that raise wall stress (hypertension, dilation, obstruction) increase oxygen consumption, straining ischemic hearts.
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: An acute afterload increase in a failing ventricle most directly causes:
options: Reduced EF and forward stroke volume
questions.explanation: A weak ventricle has little reserve against rising resistance: ESV climbs, EF falls, and forward output drops — the hemodynamic logic behind afterload reduction in acute pulmonary edema.
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a component of afterload?
questions.explanation: EDV is the principal determinant of preload. Afterload is composed of vascular resistance, arterial compliance, and outflow obstruction during systole.
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: On echocardiography, RV afterload is estimated by:
options: Measuring the tricuspid regurgitant jet velocity to derive RV systolic pressure (RVSP)
questions.explanation: Applying the simplified Bernoulli equation to the TR jet (4v²) plus RA pressure estimates RV systolic pressure — the echo surrogate for pulmonary artery pressure and RV afterload.
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: A TR jet velocity of 3.5 m/s (gradient ~49 mmHg) plus RA pressure of 10 mmHg indicates an RVSP of approximately 59 mmHg, suggesting:
questions.explanation: RVSP near 60 mmHg is well above the normal ~25 mmHg PA systolic pressure, indicating substantial pulmonary hypertension and RV pressure overload.
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: The echocardiographic hallmark of longstanding systemic hypertension is:
options: Concentric LV hypertrophy with increased relative wall thickness
questions.explanation: Chronic pressure overload produces uniform wall thickening with preserved or reduced cavity size: concentric remodeling/hypertrophy, often with LA enlargement and diastolic dysfunction.
tags: Afterload and Systemic Versus Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: The concept of "afterload mismatch" refers to:
options: The normal relationship between HR and BP
A fall in stroke volume caused by an abrupt rise in afterload that outstrips the ventricle's compensatory mechanisms
questions.explanation: When resistance rises acutely (e.g., hypertensive crisis, PE), a ventricle with limited reserve cannot instantly boost contractility or preload enough to maintain SV — output falls until compensation develops. ---
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: Inotropy refers to:
options: The volume of blood in the ventricle before contraction
The intrinsic contractile strength of the myocardium, independent of preload and afterload
The resistance the ventricle ejects against
The speed of AV nodal conduction
questions.explanation: Inotropy (contractility) is the heart's contractile performance at any given preload and afterload — the third pillar of stroke volume determination alongside preload and afterload.
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: An increase in contractility produces which combination of changes?
options: Increased stroke volume with a decreased end-systolic volume
No change in ESV or SV
questions.explanation: A stronger ventricle empties more completely: ESV falls and SV rises. This is reflected on the PV loop as a steeper ESPVR.
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: Which of the following is a positive inotrope?
questions.explanation: Dobutamine is a β1-agonist that increases contractility (and heart rate). Beta-blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are negative inotropes.
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: Myocardial ischemia affects contractility by:
options: Depressing inotropy — impaired energy production reduces cross-bridge cycling
Having no effect unless infarction occurs
questions.explanation: Ischemic myocardium produces less ATP and suffers calcium-handling impairment, so the affected region contracts weakly; significant ischemia reduces global contractility and stroke volume.
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: Cardiac output is calculated as:
questions.explanation: CO = HR × SV (e.g., 75 × 70 mL = 5.25 L/min). It is the volume of blood pumped per minute and the heart's fundamental performance index.
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: A patient has a stroke volume of 70 mL and a heart rate of 75 bpm. Cardiac output is:
questions.explanation: CO = 0.070 L × 75 = 5.25 L/min — a normal resting adult output of approximately 5 L/min.
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: The cardiac index adjusts cardiac output for body size by dividing by:
questions.explanation: Cardiac index = CO ÷ BSA, with a normal range of roughly 2.5–4.2 L/min/m², allowing fair comparison between large and small patients.
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: The normal resting cardiac output for an average adult is approximately:
questions.explanation: ~5 L/min is normal at rest; it rises with exercise up to 4–6-fold in trained individuals, driven by both heart rate and stroke volume.
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: Ejection fraction equals:
questions.explanation: EF expresses the proportion of the filled volume that is ejected per beat, integrating preload, afterload, and contractility into one clinical index of systolic performance.
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: The three determinants of stroke volume are:
options: Heart rate, conduction velocity, and blood viscosity
Valvular area, blood volume, and hemoglobin
questions.explanation: Stroke volume is governed by how much the ventricle is filled (preload), the resistance it ejects against (afterload), and the force of contraction itself (inotropy).
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: Using the Fick principle, cardiac output equals:
questions.explanation: CO = oxygen consumption ÷ (arterial − mixed venous O2 content). This direct method underlies the invasive determination of cardiac output in catheterization labs.
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: Doppler-derived stroke volume is calculated as:
options: LVOT VTI × LVOT cross-sectional area (× heart rate for cardiac output)
questions.explanation: The Doppler stroke volume is the cylindrical column of blood moved per beat: the velocity-time integral through the LVOT multiplied by its cross-sectional area; multiplying by HR gives cardiac output.
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: The LVOT diameter measures 2.0 cm. The LVOT cross-sectional area is approximately:
questions.explanation: Area = πr² = 3.14 × (1.0)² ≈ 3.14 cm². Accurate diameter measurement matters because area varies with the square of the radius — small errors are squared.
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: Sympathetic stimulation of the heart via β1 receptors produces:
options: Decreased contractility and decreased heart rate
Increased contractility and increased heart rate
Increased contractility with decreased heart rate
Decreased contractility with increased heart rate
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine acting on β1 receptors is both positively inotropic and chronotropic, raising stroke volume and cardiac output during stress or exercise.
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: Digoxin increases contractility by:
options: Inhibiting the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase, indirectly raising intracellular calcium availability to the contractile apparatus
questions.explanation: Digitalis blocks the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, raising intracellular Na⁺, which reverses the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger and increases sarcoplasmic reticular calcium — enhancing systolic force (positive inotropy).
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: The Bowditch effect (treppe) describes:
options: The fall in contractility with ischemia
The increase in contractility that occurs with an increase in heart rate
questions.explanation: As heart rate rises, more calcium enters per unit time and SR loading improves, so contractile force increases — a rate-dependent inotropy that partially offsets reduced filling time.
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: The dominant physiologic regulator of inotropy in healthy humans is:
options: Sympathetic β1-adrenergic stimulation from cardiac nerves and circulating catecholamines
questions.explanation: Sympathetic stimulation via β1 receptors is the primary physiologic mechanism increasing contractility; vagal (muscarinic) influence on ventricular inotropy is comparatively weak.
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: Dobutamine stress echocardiography assesses:
options: Contractile reserve — the ability of the ventricle to increase function with inotropic stimulation
questions.explanation: Infused dobutamine challenges the heart to increase contractility and rate; failure to augment wall motion identifies ischemia or exhausted contractile reserve (viability assessment).
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: On echocardiography, enhanced contractility is reflected by:
options: A dilated LV with low EF
An increased ejection fraction and a steeper LV dP/dt
questions.explanation: Stronger contraction produces faster pressure rise (dP/dt, measurable from the MR jet) and a higher EF; hyperdynamic states also show brisk wall motion and increased VTI.
tags: Inotropy, Cardiac Output, and Stroke Volume Determinants

questions.stem: An EF of 20% with a dilated LV and low cardiac output indicates:
options: Afterload excess as the sole problem
questions.explanation: A dilated ventricle ejecting only one-fifth of its volume reflects profoundly impaired inotropy — the systolic heart failure phenotype requiring inotropic/afterload-directed management. ---
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: The Frank–Starling mechanism is best summarized as:
options: Stroke volume is fixed regardless of filling
Higher afterload always raises stroke volume
Within physiologic limits, the ventricle ejects a larger stroke volume when it is filled more (greater end-diastolic fiber length)
questions.explanation: The intrinsic length–tension relationship lets each ventricle match its output to its inflow beat-by-beat without any external neural or hormonal input.
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: The cellular mechanism underlying the Frank–Starling relationship is:
options: Optimal actin–myosin overlap at increased sarcomere length, producing more effective cross-bridge interactions
questions.explanation: Stretching toward the optimal sarcomere length (~2.0–2.2 µm) maximizes actin–myosin overlap and myofilament calcium sensitivity, so more cross-bridges cycle and force increases.
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: The descending limb of the Starling curve (where SV falls despite higher preload) occurs when:
options: The ventricle is overstretched beyond optimal sarcomere overlap, as in severe volume overload
questions.explanation: Extreme dilation (e.g., massive regurgitation, severe overload) puts sarcomeres beyond their optimal length, reducing overlap and force — SV paradoxically drops as EDV climbs.
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: In heart failure, the ventricular function (Starling) curve is characteristically:
options: Shifted downward and to the right — less stroke volume at any given preload
Shifted upward and to the left
questions.explanation: The failing ventricle delivers less output for any filling pressure; to maintain CO it operates at higher filling pressures, which is why congestion (pulmonary edema) accompanies low output.
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: A hypovolemic patient sits at which location on the Starling curve?
options: The low-preload, low-output portion of the steep limb — highly responsive to fluid
No position, since the curve does not apply
questions.explanation: Low venous return places the ventricle on the steep rising limb, where small increases in preload produce large SV gains — the rationale for fluid resuscitation.
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: Normal systemic arterial blood pressure is approximately:
questions.explanation: 120/80 mmHg is the standard reference for normal systemic arterial pressure, generated by LV ejection against SVR; 25/10 is pulmonary, 0–4 right atrial, and 8–10 left atrial.
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: The major determinants of myocardial oxygen demand (MVO2) are:
options: Wall tension (pressure × radius), heart rate, and contractility
questions.explanation: Wall stress, rate, and inotropy consume the bulk of myocardial oxygen. Interventions that lower pressure, shrink cavity size, slow the rate, or reduce contractility all decrease MVO2.
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: Which hemodynamic combination would most dramatically increase myocardial oxygen demand?
options: Tachycardia with hypertension and enhanced contractility
Resting sinus rhythm with normal pressures
questions.explanation: Rate, pressure (wall tension), and inotropy all rise together in this scenario, multiplying MVO2 — a dangerous combination for a patient with coronary stenosis.
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: Coronary blood flow to the left ventricle occurs predominantly:
questions.explanation: Systolic intramyocardial pressure squeezes the intramural coronary vessels shut; LV perfusion therefore occurs mainly in diastole — the phase that tachycardia eliminates first.
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: Tachycardia predisposes to myocardial ischemia because it simultaneously:
options: Increases oxygen demand (rate × wall tension) while decreasing supply (shortened diastolic perfusion)
Has no effect on the supply–demand balance
questions.explanation: A fast heart raises MVO2 and shortens the diastolic window during which coronary flow occurs, squeezing the supply–demand ratio from both directions.
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: According to the lecture's key takeaways, diastole supports:
questions.explanation: Diastole is the relaxation-and-filling half of the cycle; systole is the contraction-and-ejection half. Each half has distinct pressure, volume, and valve signatures.
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: Matching the takeaway triad: preload reflects ______, afterload reflects ______, and inotropy reflects ______.
questions.explanation: Preload mainly reflects ventricular filling, afterload reflects ejection resistance, and inotropy reflects myocardial contractile strength — the conceptual framework for analyzing any hemodynamic problem.
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: Following a large anterior MI, the immediate drop in stroke volume is primarily explained by:
options: Acute loss of contractile tissue and reduced inotropy
questions.explanation: Infarcted myocardium does not contract; the ventricle's contractile strength falls at any given load, reducing SV and CO until compensation (SNS, Frank–Starling) and remodeling occur.
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: In tamponade, stroke volume falls despite hypercontractile myocardium because:
options: Preload is restricted by external pericardial pressure compressing the chambers
questions.explanation: Pericardial pressure chokes venous return and filling; even a strong ventricle cannot eject what it cannot fill. This demonstrates that preload restriction alone can collapse output.
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: In chronic severe mitral regurgitation, the ejection fraction may appear normal while forward cardiac output is reduced. Why?
options: The EF overestimates contractility because part of each ejected volume flows backward into the low-pressure left atrium
The EF is unrelated to output
questions.explanation: In MR, "ejection" includes the regurgitant fraction going into the LA rather than the aorta. A "normal" EF can therefore mask diminished forward SV and depressed true contractile function.
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: A patient in atrial fibrillation has a beat-to-beat variation in blood pressure because:
options: The irregular, loss-of-atrial-kick rhythm produces variable filling (preload) and therefore variable stroke volumes
The LV contracts twice per beat
questions.explanation: AF produces randomly variable R–R intervals; beats following short cycles fill less (lower preload, smaller SV) than beats following long pauses — producing the irregular pulse and variable BP.
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: Elderly patients with stiff ventricles tolerate new-onset atrial fibrillation poorly because:
options: They depend heavily on the atrial kick to fill noncompliant ventricles, and its loss plus shortened diastole markedly reduces EDV and CO
questions.explanation: Age-related ventricular stiffness makes the atrial contribution (20–30% or more) essential; losing it in AF drops output sharply — the reason AF often presents with decompensation in the elderly.
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: Which conditions are high-output states that increase cardiac output above ~5 L/min?
options: Anemia, arteriovenous fistula, sepsis, and hyperthyroidism
questions.explanation: Reduced viscosity/anemic hypoxia, shunting, vasodilatory infection, and thyrotoxic metabolism all demand increased flow; the heart responds with elevated CO (and, chronically, can develop high-output failure).
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: A well-trained athlete has a resting heart rate of 45 bpm yet maintains a normal cardiac output because:
options: The athlete's large stroke volume (~110–120 mL) compensates for the slow rate
questions.explanation: Endurance training enlarges LV cavity and stroke volume, so CO = SV × HR remains ~5 L/min despite bradycardia — an enlarged, efficient pump rather than a weak one.
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration

questions.stem: A patient has EDV 110 mL, ESV 40 mL, and heart rate 80 bpm. Which set of values is correct?
questions.explanation: SV = 110 − 40 = 70 mL; EF = 70 ÷ 110 ≈ 64%; CO = 0.070 × 80 = 5.6 L/min. All three values are within normal limits — a normally functioning ventricle. --- *End of question bank — Lecture 8: Cardiac Function and Hemodynamics. 200 questions.*
tags: Frank–Starling, Myocardial Oxygen Demand, and Integration
